what_its_for: Levetiracetam is used to help control seizures in people with epilepsy. It can be used alone or along with other seizure medicines. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take levetiracetam exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. Swallow tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them unless your doctor says it is okay. If you are taking the dissolving tablet (Spritam), place it on your tongue, take a sip of liquid, and swallow. If you are taking the liquid form, use the measuring device that came with your medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Take it at the same times every day to keep the medicine working well.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your age, weight, kidney function, and the type of seizures you have. Do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Stopping suddenly can cause more seizures. Adults are often started on a lower dose that is slowly increased over time.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for the one you missed. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store levetiracetam tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking levetiracetam — it can make dizziness and sleepiness worse. Be careful driving, operating machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid stopping the medicine suddenly without your doctor's guidance, as this can trigger more seizures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: new or worsening depression, thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide, unusual mood changes or aggressive behavior, extreme confusion or agitation, signs of a serious allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, fever with swollen lymph nodes or sores in your mouth, or if your seizures get worse or happen more often. Also call if you develop signs of low red blood cell counts such as unusual tiredness or pale skin.
when_it_works: Levetiracetam starts working fairly quickly, but it may take several weeks to find the right dose and see the best seizure control. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better or have not had a seizure — it works best when taken every day as prescribed.
special_populations: Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose will be based on the child's weight. Make sure doses are measured carefully. Older adults: You may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and confusion. Use caution to avoid falls. Kidney problems: Your doctor may lower your dose if your kidneys do not work well, because this medicine is removed from your body through the kidneys. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before taking or stopping this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Stopping seizure medicine during pregnancy can be dangerous, but the medicine may also carry some risks. Breastfeeding: Levetiracetam can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the best option for you and your baby.
